turns.en: Yeah. Well, I guess for podcast listeners, we'll have to get an image somewhere. This idea of flexibility versus perfection, and then regardless, celebration, is core to how we think about the streak. Because I think for the streak for us, it's very much a bend not break. If you're going to miss a day, I'd rather you come back, having missed that day, to an intact streak, but if you don't have to miss a day, I'd much rather you don't, I'd much rather you come back and use the app every day. So, that thing on flexibility though, that's almost certainly been the biggest, from a mechanic perspective, the biggest DAU driver. One of the earliest experiments we ran was going from you used to only be able to have one streak freeze and then we let you have either two or three. So, we tested two different arms. It was, again, another huge DAU win. (00:47:12): This actually is funny, it was something that... And this is, again, a callback to that growth model post from Jorge. It actually was really bad for CURR because we were basically saying, hey, you can take a day off, and that's okay, but it was really good for, this is going to be like Alphabet Soup, [inaudible 00:47:31], a weekly active user return rate. So, basically, users who had taken a day off, we were getting them to come back more at higher rates, and so it made up for our losses in CURR. But effectively, what this meant is that, why two streak freezes work better than one was, I don't know, sometimes people just need a little bit more flexibility than one day. But again, the really interesting insight of this experiment was that three streak freezes was actually no better than two streak freezes. And there were two competing things here, and I think this is important if you're going to build a streak to figure out what your flexibility mechanic is. (00:48:03): We were getting more users to return after longer times away to an intact streak. But if you start taking three days off from any habit, it's just going to be less likely that you return even four days later. And so, we had these competing things where more users might be returning to a streak, but a lot of users were also just not coming back, we were training them to take more time off. So, that flexibility, what's the right amount of... We've again, this is another area we've run hundreds of experiments on, what is the right amount of flexibility? And we are constantly surprised here. I still don't have the answer for at every point in your streak journey how much flexibility you need. One thing that I can say with certainty though is, give more flexibility when a user is starting their streak. Again, one of our biggest streak freeze experiment wins... I feel like I'm constantly saying this, one of our biggest wins, but they all were really, really big. (00:48:59): One of our biggest streak freeze wins was when you start a new streak, we give you two streak freezes. And again, it's so funny to think back, it's like how are we not doing this to begin with? But at the time, the streak freeze was an overly gamified mechanic, you had to buy them with gems, that's our in-app currency, because we wanted the whole idea of this to feel like it was really something you earned, that there was a little bit of pain to getting that streak freeze. And so, we tested though, what if we just give users when they start off their streak two streak freezes, and holy smokes to that win. (00:49:33): And it's sort of obvious now, in retrospect, but if you have a one or a two or a three-day streak, it's really easy just to let it die and restart, again, you need to get to seven days, what we've seen in the data, for it to really lock in. And so, giving users more flexibility so that it's harder to lose their streak initially, and then conversely, and this is what we keep learning, eventually, once people get on long streaks, you don't want to give them as much flexibility. Because there's a lot of times where, yeah, users don't... And I'm like this, I've got a 400-day streak. Note that that is a lot less time than I've been at Duolingo, I have lost and restarted streaks a lot of times at my time at Duolingo. (00:50:14): But you start getting on long streaks, and you really care about this feature, you really care about your streak. And most people, as long as you're not backpacking through, I don't know, the back country of Utah, you'll be in a place where you can get service. And so, figuring out who is the user that actually could use Duolingo, and not conditioning them to start taking days off that they didn't otherwise need to do is important to figure out where that line is for your feature.
turns.zh:
是啊。不过对于播客听众来说，我们得找个地方放个图片。灵活性与完美主义之间的平衡，以及无论如何都要庆祝的理念，是我们看待连续日志挑战（streak）的核心观点。因为对我来说，连续日志挑战更多是一种“灵活坚持”而非“一味完美”。如果你某天没能坚持，我们宁愿你回来后能继续保持原有的连续日志，但如果你本就不必错过一天，我当然更希望你能每天都使用应用。所以，灵活性这个点，从机制层面来说，无疑是日活跃用户（DAU）增长的最大驱动力之一。我们最早做的一个实验是，用户原本只能冻结连续日志一次，后来我们允许他们冻结两次或三次。我们测试了两种方案，结果又一次带来了DAU的大幅增长。（00:47:12）：说起来挺有意思的，这件事……这又让我想起豪尔赫那篇关于增长模型的帖子。当时对CURR（用户留存率）的影响其实很不利，因为我们当时告诉用户：嘿，你可以休息一天，这没关系。但对周活跃用户（DAU）回流率的影响却非常显著。那些休息一天的用户，回流率明显更高，这弥补了CURR的损失。但从本质上讲，两个连续日志冻结比一个更好的原因，我也不确定，也许有时候人们确实需要比一天更灵活的调整。不过这次实验最有趣的发现是，三个连续日志冻结实际上并不比两个更有效果。两者存在竞争关系，我认为这对构建连续日志机制的人来说，理解灵活性机制至关重要。（00:48:03）：我们让更多用户在离开后较长时间内重返完整的连续日志。但如果你开始每周三天休息某个习惯，四天后回来的概率就会大大降低。这里存在两种矛盾的需求：更多用户回归连续日志，但大量用户却不再回来。我们无形中在培养他们休假的习惯。所以灵活性到底该设定多大呢？这又是一个我们做了数百次实验的领域。正确的灵活性设置到底是什么？我们至今仍在探索。不过可以确定的是，在用户刚开始连续日志之旅时，给予更多灵活性会更有效果。（00:48:59）：我们最成功的连续日志冻结实验之一，是让新用户一开始就能获得两个连续日志冻结。现在回想起来，真是让人感到好笑，我们当初为什么不这么做呢？但当时连续日志冻结是一个过度游戏化的机制，需要用宝石购买（宝石是我们的应用内货币），因为我们希望用户觉得这是自己努力得来的，获得连续日志冻结需要付出一点代价。于是我们测试了让新用户一开始就能获得两个连续日志冻结，结果效果惊人。
重新开始的话，你需要坚持七天。根据我们的数据分析，只有达到这个时长才能真正巩固成果。因此，我们需要给予用户更多灵活性，避免他们在初期就轻易失去连胜记录。反过来，正如我们不断总结的经验，当用户进入长期连胜阶段后，就不宜再给予过多灵活性了。因为很多时候，用户确实会……比如我现在就有400天的连胜记录。但要知道，这远远比不上我在Duolingo的使用时长——在Duolingo的这段时间里，我多次失去并重新开始连胜记录。（00:50:14）但当你进入长期连胜阶段后，你会格外珍视这个功能，也会非常在意自己的连胜记录。大多数用户，只要不是在偏远地区，比如犹他州的偏远地区旅行，都能获得网络信号。因此，关键在于要准确判断谁是真正需要Duolingo服务的用户，而不是让他们养成不必要地休假的习惯。这样才能找到功能设计的合理平衡点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is fascinating. You can also buy a streak, right? With money. That's a feature, right?
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。你也可以花钱买连胜吧？对吧？这就是个特色功能，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah. And it's funny, this is also something that we [inaudible 00:50:54]-
turns.zh: 是啊。有趣的是，这也是我们（听不清00:50:54）——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You can buy a freeze, sorry, not a streak.
turns.zh: 你可以买连胜冻结，但不是连胜。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah. So, you can buy a streak freeze, and the way it works is you can buy gems, and then you can use those gems to buy a streak... And this is something we wrestle with. We're actively working on an experiment, right now that's having a small hit to revenue, but it's a really nice win for retention, and I think it's actually worth thinking about from day one, as you're building a streak, do you see this more as a monetization feature, or do you see this more as a retention feature? What's the role of monetization in this? What's the role of retention? And I think for us it started out much more organically, and so we have a lot of monetization hooks, that again, is the retention PM, I would love to get rid of. But again, it's sort of part of how the streak works right now. And so, we always have this tension of, hey, if we start to make it harder to buy streak freezes, then fewer people buy them, buy gems to buy them, and so there's this more convoluted series of impacts that happen.
turns.zh: 对。所以，你可以买连胜冻结，具体操作是先购买宝石，再用宝石购买连胜……这确实是个难题。我们目前正在积极测试这个功能，虽然它会对营收产生一定影响，但对留存率提升效果显著。我觉得从一开始就应该考虑：你把连胜看作是变现功能，还是留存功能？变现在这其中起什么作用？留存又扮演什么角色？对我们来说，最初的思路更偏向自然发展，所以我们设计了很多变现路径，但现在留存PM很想把这些路径去掉。不过这些机制确实是连胜机制的核心部分。所以我们一直面临这样的矛盾：如果让购买连胜冻结变得更困难，买的人就会减少，转而购买宝石来获得连胜，这样一来会产生一系列复杂的连锁反应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, no, I love that people wanting to buy streak freeze is like the ultimate sign of how much streaks matter.
turns.zh: 是啊，不，我觉得人们愿意花钱买连胜冻结，这恰恰说明连胜对用户有多重要。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, streak freeze is the other big one that we've recently demonetized, or introduced a free option for, is getting back a lost streak. So, used to lose a streak, we had a feature, in the day, back in the day, called Streak Repair, we'd give you your streak back, you had to pay gems. But what we found that worked way better was a feature called Earn Back, and this is basically where you would have to do a certain number of lessons, as long as you came back within a window soon after losing your streak, do a few lessons and we just give you your streak back. And that was such a retention winner. And again, what we thought about was it feels like you've earned it so much more when you've done... You deserve to have your streak back, we haven't cheapen the streak because you've done something. (00:52:44): And in this sense, this idea of cheapening the streak is something, like from a philosophical... Philosophy of the streak. From a philosophical level, we wrestle with all the time, of, cool, we're giving out more streak freezes, at what point do we cross the line and users start to realize their streak means nothing? Now, everything that we've seen, users are totally cool with using streak freezes and still thinking about their streak is this meaningful thing, but my co-lead, Antonia, who made that awesome cross-stitch for me, she is the keeper for us of the sanctity of the streak. And a lot of times as we... And I think this is really important to have, as you're thinking about building your streak. You can almost always get engagement wins, up to a certain point, by just cheapening the streak, making it easier to extend, letting users have more flexibility, but you kind of got to hold the line at some point. (00:53:30): And it's not clear where that line is. And once you... You talk about one-way doors or two-way doors, there's a point where you go too far and it's a one-way door, and all of a sudden those users, those 9 million users on one-year streaks don't care about their streak anymore. And that is, I don't know, again, retention PM perspective, that'd be an extinction level event for us. I don't want all of these users to stop caring about their streak. And so, to have somebody who is invested in the sanctity of this streak, and for us it's Antonia and Luis, he's very good about this, is really important, just so you make sure you don't go too far.
turns.zh:
是的，连胜冻结是我们最近取消了其货币化功能，或者推出了免费选项的另一个重要举措。以前用户丢失连胜时，我们有一个功能，叫做“连胜修复”，用户需要花费宝石来恢复连胜。但我们发现，更有效的做法是推出“赚回连胜”功能，只要用户在连胜丢失后不久重新登录并完成一定数量的课程，我们就会恢复他们的连胜。这项功能对用户留存效果显著。我们的核心理念是，用户通过努力获得的连胜才更有意义。我们从未贬低连胜的价值。

（00:52:44）：在这种情况下，降低连胜价值的做法从哲学层面来说是个挑战。我们一直在思考，随着连胜冻结次数的增加，用户何时会意识到连胜已经失去意义？从我们观察到的数据来看，用户完全接受连胜冻结机制，并认为连胜依然有意义。但我的联合负责人安东尼娅为我制作了那个很棒的十字绣，她是我们团队中连胜神圣性的守护者。我们在设计连胜机制时，必须把握好尺度。（00:53:30）：目前尚不清楚这个尺度在哪里。就像一扇双向门，当你越过界限，用户——比如那些保持一年连胜的900万用户——就会彻底失去对连胜的兴趣。这对我们来说无异于灭顶之灾。我不希望这些用户对连胜失去兴趣。因此，团队中像安东尼娅和路易斯这样坚守连胜神圣性的人至关重要，这样才能确保我们不会越界。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome insight. So, to protect... And push notifications I think are another example of this in general for companies, how much is too much? Because everyone is just like, let's just send another push, it's fine, just one more. And so, your solution to that is a person is like the keeper, and almost the gatekeeper, plus the founder, of how far is too far.
turns.zh: 这真是深刻的见解。那么，如何保护……关于推送通知，我认为这对公司来说也是一个普遍的挑战，什么时候算过度？因为大家都觉得，再发一条推送消息无伤大雅，再多一条也无妨。所以，你的解决方案是设立一个守门人——或者说看门人——以及创始人来界定这个界限。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: It's good if you can have that. I think push notifications are also easier because there's a lot of things you can do around, all right, we'll send a budget cap for how many notifications we'll send, you can-
turns.zh: 这确实很棒。如果能有这样一个角色就好了。我认为推送通知相对容易控制，因为有很多技术手段可以实现，比如设定发送通知的预算上限，限制发送次数等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like [inaudible 00:54:38] policy.
turns.zh: 这就像[00:54:38不可听清]政策。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, policies. But I think with a lot of things, at least for the streak, it's harder to create policies for in the same way, a lot of it has to be done based on feel, and so you just got to use your best judgment at times.
turns.zh: 是的，制定政策确实困难。至少对于连胜机制来说，很难用固定规则来规范，很多决策必须基于直觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Okay. Any other, maybe one or two more lessons from this journey of what streaks has become today.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。关于 streaks 如今发展历程的其他心得，或许再分享一两个经验吧。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: You mentioned notifications, and I've mentioned this a few times. One... It's funny, you tend to think of, exactly as you say, you can just always send another notification, it's going to be some win, and at some point it'll be a bad experience, but it's tough to see that. There's actually a notification that we... So, we send two notifications related to your core streak each day, the first is a practice reminder, we send it, this is actually an interesting insight, 23 and a half hours after you practice the day before. Whoa, that is a lot.
turns.zh: 你提到了通知，我也多次谈到这个话题。首先... 很有意思的是，你总会觉得，嗯，正如你所说，随时发送新的通知就能带来成功，但有时结果却适得其反。这其实挺难看清的。我们现在发送的每日核心 streak 相关的通知有两个，第一个是练习提醒，我们会在你前一天练习结束后的23个半小时后发送。哇，这时间间隔可真长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 23 and a half. Okay,
turns.zh: 23个半小时。好的，

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: So, basically, if you practice at noon today, we'll send it to you at 11:30 AM tomorrow, and we have done-
turns.zh: 基本上，如果你今天中午练习，我们会在明天上午11:30给你发送通知。我们之前让用户自己设定练习提醒时间，但后来发现——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's, because it's like assuming they are free in that time the day before, maybe they'll be free at the same time?
turns.zh: 用户可能前一天没空，可能当天有其他安排？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: And we actually moved, we used to let users set this practice reminder time, and our thinking was, cool, you're going to say 7:00 PM, that's when I really want to extend my streak each day, and then you know what? I say this to somebody with two kids, life gets in the way, life always gets in the way, and when you think you're going to practice will change, your life will change, whatever. And what we realize is the best indicator of when you should practice was when did you practice the day before. We could almost certainly get more detailed, we have tried a bunch of ways to have much more complex logic, and what always wins is 23 and a half hours.
turns.zh: 所以我们改了，以前让用户自己设定提醒时间，但后来发现最有效的提醒时间其实是前一天练习结束后的时间。我们尝试过更复杂的逻辑，但最终发现23个半小时最合适。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. Revealed behavior versus stated.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。行为揭示胜过用户自述。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So, again, we send this practice reminder 23 and a half hours later, the other thing that we'll do though is we'll send a, what we call a streak saver, and this is at 10:00 at night, if you have not extended your streak, we'll send you a message saying, hey, it's your last chance, this is it, if you don't extend your streak. And you would think that, that's kind of spammy, that's kind of annoying, to get a notification from an app at 10:00 PM, but what we found is because people care about their streak, their streak is this good thing that they attach positive emotions, that they don't really want to lose, that notification reminding them, hey, come back and... People see this by and large as a positive notification and not a negative notification. (00:56:53): Obviously, it serves our purpose as well of getting users to come back and not lose their streaks, but again, I think if you can think about your notification strategy related to what is the feature that it's tied to, how do users perceive that? You can almost certainly, not get away with more, but you can be thoughtful about notification load, and when to send notifications, and again, for us, this late night message, that's also highly impactful, super good, is actually something that could be perceived as spammy, but a lot of our users really do... Somebody who, it's often late at night, and I work here, and I'm like, oh, forgot to do my... I was think about Duolingo all day, here it is, 11:15, and I still haven't done it, that message is really powerful.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以我们现在在23个半小时后发送练习提醒，另外我们还会发送一个叫“streak saver”的通知，晚上10点发送，如果你当天没能延续 streak，就会收到一条消息，提醒你这是最后的机会了。你可能会觉得晚上10点收到 app 通知挺烦人的，但我们发现因为用户很在意他们的 streak，把它当作积极的事物，不愿意失去它，所以这种通知反而被视为正面提醒而非负面干扰。（00:56:53）显然，这对我们也很有用，能促使用户回来，避免 streak 断掉。但还是要考虑通知策略与产品功能的关联，用户对此的感知如何。比如我们深夜发送的这条消息，效果就非常好，用户反响很积极。（00:58:21）有时候我也会遇到这种情况，晚上很晚了，比如我在这里工作，会想，哎呀，忘了做练习了，整天都在想 Duolingo，11:15了还没做，这条消息真的很有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It has saved me many times, I totally know that message, and I love that it's a late night message from an app, very rarely do you actually, are happy about that, and I love that this actually is a good example where-
turns.zh: 是啊。这救过我好多次，我完全懂那个提醒，而且我特别喜欢这条来自应用的深夜通知——很少有人会对这种情况感到开心，但我觉得这恰恰是个很好的例子，说明——

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: It's really funny, all of the stories that you hear about people extending their streak, if you look around a Duolingo party, where it's like 11:30, 11:45, all the Duolingo employees, they're are doing their lesson at the last minute. You always see these pictures of people in the club doing, or at a concert doing Duolingo, and yeah, because it's like otherwise you're going to use a streak freezer, or God forbid you will lose your streak.
turns.zh: 太搞笑了，那些关于用户延续连胜纪录的故事。比如在Duolingo聚会上，大家都是11点半、11点45分才开始学习，所有员工都在最后一刻赶着完成课程。还有那些在夜店、音乐会上玩Duolingo的照片，哈哈，因为不然你就得用连胜冻结功能了，更别提连胜失败的后果了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so funny. Okay, anything else? And if there's more than one more, definitely share, but any other really interesting lessons or wrong turns or insights?
turns.zh: 太逗了。好的，还有什么想分享的吗？如果不止一个故事，欢迎多聊聊，但有没有其他特别有趣的学习经历、翻车瞬间或者深刻见解？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: I talked about streak freezes, and we've done a lot with streak freeze, but I think if you're going to make flexibility a thing, it's probably also useful thinking about how do you celebrate perfection. And so, we have a feature that we have, it is the simplest thing in the world, it's called Perfect Streak. And it's just, if you don't use the streak freeze for a few days, we make your streak look gold, and we make your little progress bar on the calendar just look a little bit nicer. There's no reward for doing it, you don't get anything other than this nice little indication, and it is awesome. It is a simple feature, it is ultra not complex, and it is really powerful, not only for getting users to, as a bit of a reward, they'd be hey, get to seven days without using a streak freeze and your streak becomes perfect, but it's also a really nice indication of users who aren't using streak freezes. (00:59:14): Here is the thing that if you don't use a streak freeze, which, again candidly, I would love for you never to use a streak freeze, if you don't use a streak freeze, your streak will stay perfect. It's funny, we actually just, we're constantly responding to bug reports about the streak. It is... I swear to God, we have the best infrastructure around this feature because it is so important. We had an employee who lost her, I think a four-month perfect streak, and it was a big deal for her because she did her lesson, and she was crossing international dateline, there was a bunch of stuff going on that was like, it was just kind of weird in our backend. But people start to care about perfection as much as they do their streak, and for that person it was a big deal when they lost their perfect streak. And so, this is just an example of, look, if you're going to go after flexibility, which is good, finding a way to pull users back into perfection is a really important counterweight to have.
turns.zh: 我之前谈到了连续天数不中断的机制，我们在这方面做了很多工作。但我认为，如果要把灵活性作为一个重点，思考如何庆祝用户的完美表现也很重要。因此，我们推出了一个简单易用的功能——“完美连胜”。只要用户几天内不使用连续天数不中断机制，我们就会将他们的连胜记录标注为金色，并让日历上的进度条显示得更美观。虽然没有任何奖励，但这种温馨的提示效果非常棒。这是一个极其简单且易于实现的功能，不仅能激励用户使用连续天数不中断机制（比如连续七天不使用，就能获得完美连胜），同时也能为那些不使用该功能的用户提供一个友好的提醒。（00:59:14）：关键在于，如果你不使用连续天数不中断机制（说实话，我希望大家永远不用这个功能），你的连胜记录会一直保持完美。有趣的是，我们经常收到关于连胜机制的bug报告。为了保障这一核心功能的稳定性，我们投入了大量精力。曾有员工失去了四个月的完美连胜记录，这对她来说意义重大——她当时正在跨越国际日期线，系统出现了一些故障。但用户对完美的执着程度丝毫不亚于对连胜机制的关注。对那位用户而言，失去完美连胜记录是件大事。这充分说明，追求灵活性固然重要，但找到方法让用户重回完美之路同样至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm imagining is you guys need a Amazon style chatbot that just gives you the streak back, it's just like, okay, here you go.
turns.zh: 我想象的是，你们需要一个亚马逊式的聊天机器人，直接把连胜记录还给用户，就像“好的，给你。”

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: We have very much... So, we have, if people lose their streak, there's ways to get in contact with us, but we've actually thought about that, where it's like, okay, we should just build a self-service feature, and if we think that your excuse is good enough, whatever, we'll just [inaudible 01:00:34].
turns.zh: 我们确实有相关措施。比如用户失去连胜记录后，可以通过多种方式联系我们，但我们也考虑过更便捷的自助服务方案。如果我们认为用户的理由合理，系统会自动处理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. [inaudible 01:00:35].
turns.zh: 是的，是的。[01:00:34不可听清]

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Because again, I'd much rather you be on a streak than have lost it, particularly [inaudible 01:00:41].
turns.zh: 嗯，再说一次，我宁愿你保持连胜状态，也不愿你失去它，尤其是[01:41:00未听清]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. But it also can feel that easy. I love this, I also love this point about just the power of the animation and user experience having impact, that's really interesting. Is that something you find often, just celebrating and making it feel really amazing without copy or any feature is just like, holy, you're awesome?
turns.zh: 好的。但有时候这确实挺容易做到的。我喜欢这个观点，也喜欢你提到的动画和用户体验的影响力，这真的很有趣。你经常会遇到这种情况吗？就是通过庆祝和营造惊喜感来提升用户体验，而不需要任何复制或额外功能——哇，你太棒了！

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: This is another thing where it's like when users care about the feature, using not only animation, haptics, sound effects, using... And it's funny, we don't have sound effects on the streak, this is probably something we'll look at in the not too distant in future, but haptics are something we have done a lot of testing on-
turns.zh: 还有一点，当用户重视某个功能时，动画、触觉反馈和音效都会发挥作用。这很有趣，我们的 streak 功能目前没有音效，但未来不久可能会考虑加上。不过我们在触觉反馈上做了很多测试——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like the phone vibrating in various ways.
turns.zh: 比如手机震动的各种效果。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, exactly, your phone, there being a really cool haptic pattern as you extend your streak, all of this stuff wins. And it's cool because I think it wins... There's a few reasons. One is it just makes you feel good, you get some cool moment in your streak, and we celebrate you, and we celebrate you in this visual way, and your phone's buzzing, it just feels awesome. The other thing it does is it causes you to pause on that screen, and I think there's this desire, as you think through a lot of, as PMs think through, oh, how can I get users through this funnel as painlessly as possible? I talked about [inaudible 01:01:52]. There's a lot of times where I don't, I want you to stop. I want you to stop and land on the screen. (01:01:56): You got to be careful not to do this for too many screens, but the one big ones, sometimes I just want you to pause there and enjoy the moment. If I can get you to enjoy the moment more, you're going to care more about your streak, and you're going to be coming back tomorrow. And so, animations that are cool, and that cause you to really soak it in, haptics that feel good, all of that comes together to make you really focus on that moment, all of that just gets users more connected to their streak. So, animation in the right times works well and it's something we've had win quite a lot.
turns.zh: 对呀，完全正确！当你延续 streak 时，手机震动并伴有酷炫的触觉反馈，这些设计元素都非常加分。这很棒，因为我觉得它能带来几个好处。一是能提升用户体验，让你获得美好的时刻，我们会用视觉效果和震动反馈来庆祝你的成功。（01:56）有时候你得小心别在太多界面用这种设计，但关键的几个界面，我希望你能停下来，享受这一刻。如果我能让你更享受这个过程，你就会更在意自己的 streak，明天还会继续使用。所以，恰当使用动画效果能带来积极效果，我们在这方面确实收获颇丰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who designs the haptic stuff? Is there a haptic designer?
turns.zh: 谁负责设计触觉反馈？有专门的触觉设计师吗？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: For the longest time it would be a product designer, or actually, it initially started as the engineer would be like, all right, would cobble together haptics, based on what they felt good, then it became a product design role, where they would use their best judgment. We actually just recently required an animation studio, Hobbs in Detroit, and now they are the sort of keepers of, they do a lot of motion design work, haptics very close to that, and so they do a lot of that. I do remember trying to hire for a while a haptics contractor, like haptics design, and it was the saddest hiring I've ever done, because it was just, I don't know, it was such a specific... I don't know. I just went through a lot of people who, it's just a really tricky space of kind of sound effects, kind of motion design, sort of technical...
turns.zh: 很长一段时间以来，都是产品设计师负责。最初，工程师会根据感觉不错的效果临时拼凑触觉反馈，后来这项工作逐渐演变成产品设计师的职责，由他们根据最佳判断进行设计。我们最近刚引入了底特律的 Hobbs 动画工作室，现在他们负责这部分工作，主要做动态设计和触觉反馈相关的工作。我记得我们曾试图招聘触觉设计师，但那是我经历过最糟糕的招聘过程，因为这实在是个太细化的领域，涵盖音效、动态设计和技术层面……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, such a unique role.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个独特的角色。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Very unique specific skill set.
turns.zh: 非常独特的专业技能组合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. And there's very few apps that really need this this deeply, so you're almost creating this person.
turns.zh: 好的。确实很少有应用需要如此深入地处理这个问题，所以你几乎是在为用户量身定制整个体验。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is fascinating. That's like a whole podcast on its own. By the way, I was going to say as you're talking about this, I love that it's a win to celebrate people that don't lose their streak, you introduce this way to make it flexible, and that's a big win, and then you go the opposite direction of, if you don't use this feature, you also feel even better.
turns.zh: 这太令人着迷了。这本身就可以单独做成一期播客。顺便说一句，你提到庆祝连续使用天数的用户是件好事，你设计了灵活的机制来实现这一点，这真是高明之举。然后你又反其道而行之——如果你不使用这个功能，用户反而会感觉更好。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Well, and it's funny, you talked about the danger of feature bloat, or we sort of talked about the danger of feature bloat, this is actually something I'm constantly thinking about with this. We have the streak, but then we also have the perfect streak, and we count how many weeks you've had a perfect streak. Well, all of a sudden we have two streak numbers that are competing with each other. It's funny, we actually don't introduce the concept of a perfect streak until after you've hit seven days, and some of this is just because the cognitive load of additional streak features. A lot of our cooler streak features, you got to get on a long enough streak. And not to say we haven't tested it because we have, because we test everything, introducing these features earlier, but what we've found is that pretty universally they lose when we introduce too many things, too many concepts to users too early in the experience, it's just hard for them to manage.
turns.zh: 嗯，有趣的是，你提到了功能过载的风险，或者说我们也讨论过这个问题。这实际上是我一直在思考的难题。我们有连续使用天数的记录，但还有完美连续使用天数的统计，计算你连续使用了多少周。突然之间，这两个连续使用天数的指标开始互相竞争。有趣的是，我们直到用户连续使用了七天后才引入完美连续使用天数的概念，部分原因是额外功能会增加用户的认知负荷。我们很多更酷的连续使用天数功能，都需要用户有足够长的连续使用天数才能解锁。并不是说我们没有测试过——我们测试了所有功能——但我们发现，如果在用户体验早期就引入太多新东西、太多新概念，用户往往难以应对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, sweet. I know that we can go down this track for hours and hours, there's endless learnings about all the things you all have done along the journey. I want to shift to talking about how your team operates. So, there's a lot of threads you touched on of just how a team can do this so well, shift 600 experiments, as you said, continue to find opportunity. What are some maybe lessons or advice you'd have for folks that are like, oh wow, I want to work more like this, from your team's experience, how does your team to operate that folks can learn from?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我知道我们可以就这个话题深入探讨好几个小时，你们在产品开发过程中积累了无数宝贵经验。我想转向聊聊你们团队的运作方式。你们提到了很多要点，比如如何让团队如此高效地运作，尝试600个实验，不断寻找机会。基于你们团队的经验，你们有什么建议或经验可以分享给那些希望效仿的团队吗？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, maybe just a little bit of context. Duolingo cares a lot about... So, most of our teams are metric-based teams. So, we do the most work with streak, but the metric, what we really care about at the end of the day is CURR, and DAUs, because we see that DAUs hit CURR. And so, when you can be really laser focused on, my goal each quarter is to make this metric go up, I think it's much easier to make sure that you're working on the highest ROI thing. I think when you think more about like, oh, I want to make this feature better, I think it's easier to get lost in what better means, and how you think about better. And so, I do think that having a really strong degree of focus as a team on what is the metric that I'm caring about, and how is that directing my efforts is-
turns.zh: 是的，先讲点背景吧。Duolingo非常重视……所以我们的大多数团队都是以指标为导向的。我们在连续使用天数上投入最多精力，但最终我们真正关心的指标是活跃用户数（CURR）和每日活跃用户数（DAUs），因为我们发现DAUs能直接影响CURR。当你能高度专注于“每个季度我的目标是提升这个指标”时，确保自己在ROI最高的项目上投入精力就会容易得多。我觉得当你考虑“我想改进这个功能”时，更容易迷失在“改进”的定义和标准中。所以我认为团队能高度专注于我关心的指标，以及如何围绕它调整工作方向——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Versus feature-oriented. So, basically your teams are structured around a metric/a goal/outcome versus we own this feature, or this product.
turns.zh: 而不是以功能为导向。所以基本上，你们的团队是围绕指标/目标/结果来组织的，而不是“我负责这个功能”或“我负责这个产品”。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: So, retention owns streak, I guess, but that's only because we've seen streak drive CURR better than any feature. But we are not, we have this IAP hook with our streak freeze purchases, there are other teams that work on, that can and have worked on the streak, because it's not ours to say, no, no, no, we do all the iterations here, we just know that it drives our metric better. In the same way that leaderboards, we have a team that focuses on how much time you spent, we want users to spend more time on Duolingo so they're learning more. Leaderboards is the best vector for doing it, so that team does a lot of leaderboards work, but every now and then I have an idea that I think will be highly retentive, and I will go in, and I'll pitch to them, and then we'll do some change to the leaderboard to make it more retentive. (01:06:53): But I do think having that clear metric of we're trying to drive CURR not we're trying to just make this feature better, helps at least make sure, give the team clear marching orders, and that focus I think is really good for prioritizing backlog.
turns.zh: 好的。我觉得留存率决定了用户的连胜次数，但这只是因为我们发现连胜功能对用户参与度（CURR）的提升效果远超其他功能。不过我们并不会完全掌控这个功能——我们有通过应用内购买（IAP）锁定连胜次数的机制，其他团队也可以开发相关功能，毕竟这不完全由我们说了算。我们只是知道连胜功能能有效提升用户指标。同样，排行榜功能也是如此，我们有专门的团队负责用户停留时长优化，目标是让用户在Duolingo上花更多时间学习。排行榜是实现这一目标的最佳载体，所以团队在这方面下了很大功夫。但偶尔我也会想到一些高留存率的点子，就会去向他们提议，调整排行榜机制以提升留存率。（01:06:53）但我认为明确目标——我们要提升用户参与度（CURR），而不只是优化某个单一功能——至少能为团队指明清晰的方向。这种聚焦优先级处理积压任务的思维方式非常有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. This is a really important point, this is the same way Airbnb worked, when I worked there for a long time, is it's, here's a goal that we want your team to be responsible for, you can work on any product you need to hit this goal, as you said, often various products are most connected to what you're doing, but what you're describing is, even though a team's kind of... I imagine you own it from a [inaudible 01:07:29] perspective, and you're like are the shepherd of this part of the feature because it hits your goal, helps your goal most. But any other team can come in and be like, hey Jackson, we need to work on some streak stuff to help with learning, you're like, go for it. Just a tangent there. Do they work really closely with your team if they want to do some work in the code? How does that work logistically?
turns.zh: 不错。这确实是个关键点。Airbnb的运作方式也是如此，我在那里工作多年时发现：我们会给团队设定明确的目标，由团队自主负责达成目标。团队可以选择任何产品来达成目标，但通常与你的工作最相关的会是多个产品。不过你提到的这种情况——即使其他团队想改动代码，也需要得到你的批准。这里可能涉及软性所有权问题：我们不反对其他团队改动连胜功能，但如果我们对连胜功能有数个季度的路线图规划……我说的是可能，但实际上我们确实有。多个季度的路线图规划后，如果其他团队想改动连胜功能，我们会评估这是否与我们的计划冲突，以及如何协调。很多时候其他团队提出的改动可能基于错误的背景假设，所以我们需要简化现有流程，进行知识共享，说明我们对连胜功能的理解、成功经验和失败教训，确保改动符合我们的核心假设。总之，关键在于确保收益大于成本。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah. If you are, again, this is where I say there's soft ownership, we're not against teams doing things to the streak, but if we're going to do something given we probably have multiple quarters worth of a roadmap around the streak... I say probably, we do. Multiple quarters of roadmap for what we can do to the streak, if other teams want to come and mess with it, okay, we got to just figure out how is that going to work with what our plans for the streak were, how do we make sure a lot of times when teams are coming in thinking, hey, let's do this to the streak, they're in context that we might have, and so there's as much of a much simpler version of what we're doing now, a bit of a knowledge sharing, of saying, all right, well, this is what we think about the streak, this is what we've seen work, hasn't worked, how does that influence some of the hypothesis that you have. And so, I think getting that really... Making sure the juice is worth the squeeze.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good old-fashioned product management work right there.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。你们的运作方式还有哪些有趣之处，又是如何取得这样的成功的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. What else is interesting about how you all operate and how you all work to achieve this sort of success?
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Again, my team lead runs, Antonia runs the most... A really process, if you're going to run this experiments, you have to be really process-oriented and really thoughtful about which experiments am I going to run when, how is that going to set up the next one, there's heavy Jira automation, I think sometimes the Atlassian suite makes my eyes bleed, but there's a lot of times where that degree of process helps the team unblock engineers and make them move really fast. And so, making sure that you have really good process around how are you going to run so many experiments, it's worth investing in.
turns.zh: 再次说明，我的团队领导负责项目管理，安东尼娅负责的项目最多……说真的，要开展这些实验，你必须具备高度的流程意识，深思熟虑地规划每个实验的时机和顺序，确保后续项目能顺利衔接。Jira的自动化功能确实让人眼花缭乱，但这种严密的流程体系能有效解放工程师的生产力，让团队运转得更高效。因此，建立完善的实验管理流程绝对值得投入精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you follow that thread actually? Just when you say that, what does that look like? What are some elements of that process to make this work efficiently?
turns.zh: 你能具体解释一下这个流程吗？你刚才提到的，具体是怎样的？要确保这个流程高效运作，需要哪些关键要素？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: All the way down to, really detailed roadmaps around, all right, we're running this experiment is based on the results of this experiment, or might hook into an element of this feature, how do we make sure that we're lining up implementation on this so that as soon as this thing runs and we're ready to go, we can start rolling out the next one. I hate features just sitting around and us not, again, continuing that thread. So, it's not just thinking about what's our engineering bandwidth, but also what's the design bandwidth to make sure that we have the next iteration of this feature ready to go. We're planning months out, as we think about these feature iterations, even small ones, feature iterations, because when you lose cycles, not pushing on a feature, it's just sort of lost opportunity. And so, everything from being thoughtful about engineering roadmaps to design roadmaps to product roadmaps, all of that needs to come together in a system.
turns.zh: 一直到非常细化的路线图阶段，比如根据某个实验的结果设计下一个实验，或者接入某个功能模块，确保后续的实施工作能紧跟其后，一旦当前实验结束，就能立即启动下一个项目。我特别反感功能开发被搁置，无法延续之前的思路。所以，关键不仅在于评估工程团队的负荷，还要兼顾设计团队的能力，确保功能迭代的下一阶段能及时到位。我们的功能迭代规划甚至要提前数月筹备，哪怕是小型功能更新也如此，因为一旦错失迭代周期，就等于错失良机。从工程路线图到设计路线图，再到产品路线图，所有环节都需要在一个统一的系统中协调统一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, essentially, mapping dependencies across function, and you're saying in Jira you can do this.
turns.zh: 所以，本质上就是跨职能的依赖关系管理，而你提到在Jira中可以实现这一点。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: You can do a lot of it in Jira, there is a non-zero amount of Google Docs that we have, that sometimes does things a little bit... I don't know, sometimes it just looks a little bit nicer, it's a little more flexible.
turns.zh: Jira确实能处理很多这类需求，但我们也有不少用Google Docs完成的任务，有时Google Docs的界面更友好，更灵活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. [inaudible 01:10:38].

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: But Jira is our, it is where the motherload of process is.
turns.zh: 但Jira才是我们流程管理的核心系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. Okay. What else?
turns.zh: 好的。还有什么要补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Another thing that I'll just say is, we really resist the urge to do the big V1. And I think this is, I shared the streak goal example, where, a lot of times when we're exploring something we will say, okay, well, that's cool, how do we strip away a bunch of stuff and figure out what our core hypothesis is? And then, just ship that thing first as a V1. Because it's easy, and I've found this time and time again, it's easy to add things, features that make them win, I've worked in retention engagement long enough, I can add, I know enough things to pull, and bells to add, and whistles to make something win, but there's a lot of times where it's like cool, t [inaudible 01:11:27] because all the whistles you added, not because of what your core hypothesis was, and a lot of times if you can just really simplify what the feature is, it's also much easier to ship, it's easier to design. (01:11:37): You're not designing for a whole system, you're designing for something much simpler. And so, getting everybody to think that way, allows us to end up shipping faster, shipping simpler, designing faster, getting faster approval, getting insight, and then doing what I talked about with streak goal, being able to run iteration after iteration after iteration, add these things iteratively. And then not only by doing this are you able to move faster, but you get confidence at each step of the way, that, hey, my series of hypotheses is actually born out. Or if it's not, cool, then we're going to drop that part of the feature, and then just ship what actually matters.
turns.zh: 还有一点我要说的是，我们真的在克制自己，不去急着推出大版本的V1产品。我之前分享过连胜目标的例子，很多时候当我们探索某个方向时，会想，好吧，这想法不错，但如何去掉一些冗余功能，找到核心假设呢？然后先把这个功能作为V1版本上线。这很简单，我多次发现，要想让产品成功，添加功能其实很简单。我在留存和用户参与度领域工作多年，总能找到各种方法去优化产品，比如增加奖励机制、优化界面设计，但很多时候这些改进只是为了让产品看起来更花哨，而非真正贴近核心假设。如果能简化产品功能，设计起来也会更容易，获得审批也会更快。（01:11:37）你不需要设计整个系统，只需专注于更简单的部分。让团队都养成这种思维模式，能让我们更快上线更简洁的产品，设计更高效，获得更快速的反馈和洞察。就像连胜目标案例一样，可以不断迭代优化。这样做不仅能加速进程，还能在每一步验证假设的正确性。如果假设不成立，就果断放弃某个功能模块，专注于真正重要的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If I can try to summarize the broad lesson so far that I'm hearing, and maybe you would've shared this, but I'm just thinking, if I were to try to design a company to operate, that we all operate, you essentially map all the levers that drive the business. So, you have this mapping of all the metrics that drive up to growth and daily active users. CURR ended up being the biggest specific metric to drive growth long term, so there's imagining a tree of all the opportunities you could work on, you found this is what is most connected to our growth. You basically just start mining, I don't know if mining is the right metaphor, but just looking for things that move that specific metric. (01:13:04): You just look and poke and explore, and then once you find one, you just go real deep on trying a lot of different... You come up with a hypothesis, and a strategy of here's how we think we can do this, and how we can move this, and then you just try a bunch of stuff. There's also this element of the Arrested Development quote, "There's always money in the banana stand," comes to mind, where it's just keep working on, see there's more, there's going to be more opportunity at this.
turns.zh: 如果让我总结目前听到的核心经验（可能你也分享过），我认为如果要设计一家公司运作模式，我们都需要先梳理所有驱动业务的关键因素。比如，映射所有影响增长和日活跃用户的核心指标。最终发现CURR指标对长期增长贡献最大。换句话说，就是要构想出所有可能的增长机会树，然后找到与增长关联最紧密的那个维度。接着就开始深挖，不知道用“深挖”是否准确，但就是不断探索和尝试。一旦找到方向，就深入研究，提出假设和策略，尝试各种优化方案。这让我想起《发展受阻》里那句“香蕉摊永远有钱赚”，意思就是不断尝试，发现机会总会出现。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: When I joined Duolingo, the PM that I took over for, Anton, who used to lead the retention team, I remember saying, "Dude, the streak, it just counts up, you guys have been testing on it for years, how much more work can we do on the streak?" And he was like, Jackson, you child... He didn't say exactly this, but this is how I felt it. Like, Jackson, you child, we're not even 30% of the way optimized. And four years later, I say that with such conviction, we are so far away from... We've made a ton of strides, but we are still so far away, and every quarter where we ship a ton of wins and improvements to the streak, it just continues to prove to me that there is so much more to be done. (01:14:11): So, I think your framing of it is... And I would say there's a lot of thought that goes into, again, I talk about the strength of the hypothesis that you have to have as you start to build out larger feature strategy, I do think it's really important to not just do a bunch of random stuff but do it with intent, with a goal in mind, otherwise, you do end up in these local maximas. But yeah, there's still a bunch of stuff that we haven't tried that I think we have high confidence in working out and so we'll keep doing that.
turns.zh: 加入Duolingo时，我接手的项目经理安东曾负责留存团队。我记得他当时说：“老兄，连续天数（streak）这个功能只是在累积数字，你们已经测试了好多年了，还能在这上面再下多大功夫？”他当时的语气像是在说：“杰克逊，你个菜鸟……” 虽然他没直接这么说，但我能感受到那种无奈。就像是说：“杰克逊，你个菜鸟，我们优化得连30%都不到。” 四年后的今天，我依然深有同感——我们离目标还差得远。尽管在连续天数功能上取得了诸多进展，但差距依然巨大。每次我们在连续天数功能上推出新改进时，都让我深刻意识到还有太多工作要做。（01:14:11）：所以我觉得你对这个问题的理解……我认为这需要深思熟虑。再说一次，当你开始制定大型功能策略时，假设你有一个强有力的理论基础，这点至关重要。不能随意尝试，否则就会陷入局部最优解。但确实还有很多未尝试的方向，我们对成功充满信心，所以会继续探索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any other, say, lasting lessons from this journey that if someone were to try to operate this way, build streaks into their product, anything you'd recommend?
turns.zh: 在这段经历中，有没有其他持久的经验教训？如果有人想效仿这种模式，将连续天数功能融入产品，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, I really do think it starts with... Streaks are an engagement hack. You can make your app more retentive, I'm almost positive, almost every app out there can make it more retentive. It is loss aversion, that is, again, armchair psychologist Jackson, it's just a thing that works on humans. But if your app is not something that users want to use every day, or whatever cadence you want your app to be, to work on, it's going to be, you're only going to get so much from that streak, and honestly, it's probably going to distract you from what really should matter, which is making your app something that people want to use every day. (01:15:35): And so, if you start focusing on the streak but you haven't made that an enjoyable experience, you're just going to waste a lot of time, honestly. And so, I think making sure that you have your core loop of your app figured out, that it is giving value to users, it is something that they want to come back to every day, that really sets the stage for something to layer a streak on. So, resist the temptation, if you don't think you've reached that point, to go too hard down the path of streak.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实认为关键在于……连续天数是一种用户留存的技巧。我几乎可以肯定，市面上几乎所有应用都能通过优化留存率来提升用户粘性。其核心原理是利用人类的损失厌恶心理。但如果你开发的应用用户不常使用，或者无法形成稳定的使用习惯，连续天数功能的效果就会大打折扣。说实话，它甚至可能分散你对核心任务的注意力——让用户每天都想用你的应用才是最重要的。（01:15:35）：所以，如果你一开始就把重点放在连续天数功能上，而没有先优化核心体验，那就是在浪费时间。我的建议是，先确保应用的核心循环设计合理，能为用户创造价值，让他们乐于每天回访，这样才能为叠加连续天数功能奠定基础。所以，如果你觉得自己还没达到这个阶段，就别急于在连续天数功能上投入过多精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good point. Just like a streak is not going to solve your problems if people don't actually care about the core value you're providing.
turns.zh: 这观点很深刻。就像连续天数功能如果用户不重视你提供的核心价值，就无法解决你的问题。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: No, and honestly, it'll probably cause more problems if what you end up focusing on is how do I make the streak highly engaging, but your app is... You're wasting time that could otherwise be better spent on solving more critical problems. So, that's one learning, the other thing that I'll say is, we met with one of our board members, Bing, Bing Gordon, a few weeks, or a few months ago rather, and he had this comment where he was just like, "The reason why users care about your streak so much is because you care about your streaks much." You being Duolingo. The reason why users care about our streak so much is because Duolingo cares about the streaks so much. And we're like, what do you mean? Well, he's like, well, after every session you see a big streak screen, and it's animated cooler than almost any other screen in the app, and then sometimes you see some other screens, and there's all these other... You don't let a user forget it, you talk about them in messages. (01:17:01): And so, I think it's worth thinking about, look, if you're going to build a streak, and then you're going to [inaudible 01:17:06] it off into the corner of your app, where users aren't going to see it, they're probably not going to care about it as much, which might be fine, because there might be other levers that you think are more important to pull on, but there's a reason why we focus as much on the streak as we do, and that's because we want it to be top of mind for users. And that's not by accident then that users start to care about it. And so, I think just as you're thinking about building the streak, making sure that you're giving it the visibility it deserves, if you want it to have the kind of impact that Duolingo has, it's sort of an important hierarchy principle to think about as you design things.
turns.zh: 不会。说实话，如果你把精力都花在如何让用户对连胜记录保持高度兴趣上，而你的应用本身却……这只会浪费本可以用来解决更关键问题的宝贵时间。所以这是一个经验教训。另外，我想说的是，我们几周前或几个月前与董事会成员Bing Gordon会面时，他提到了一个观点："用户之所以如此关注连胜记录，是因为你们自身对连胜记录的重视。" 你是Duolingo，用户之所以如此在意连胜记录，是因为Duolingo本身就非常重视连胜记录。我们当时很困惑，问他这话什么意思？他回答道：每次用户完成学习任务后，你都会展示一个华丽的连胜记录界面，其动画效果比应用中其他任何界面都要酷炫得多。有时用户还会看到其他界面，但所有这些界面都强化了连胜记录的重要性。你不会让用户忘记它的存在，还会在消息中反复提及它。（01:17:01）所以我认为值得深思的是，若你要打造连胜记录功能，却把它藏在应用角落，让用户难以注意到，他们很可能就不会那么在意了。当然，可能还有其他你认为更重要的功能，但我们之所以如此重视连胜记录，是因为我们希望它能成为用户脑海中的首要记忆点。而用户之所以会如此关注它，绝非偶然。因此，在设计连胜记录功能时，务必确保它获得应有的可见度，这样才能达到Duolingo那样的影响力。这是设计过程中需要牢记的重要层次原则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point. You look for cues to the app of tell me what I should pay attention to, what's important? If you're just like fire, explosions, you made a streak, oh, maybe I should pay attention to this feature. And then the push notifications obviously encourage you there too. Anything else along those lines?
turns.zh: 这观点很棒。你需要寻找应用中的提示线索，告诉用户该关注什么、什么重要。比如，如果用户看到火焰、爆炸特效，提示他们连胜了，或许他们会留意这个功能。推送通知显然也能起到同样的效果。有没有其他类似的做法？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Maybe final thing is, look, we ran so many tests on our Duolingo streak to figure out what worked. We have a philosophy at Duolingo, of test it first. We are a lot of times willing to test things. I really think that if you're going to try to introduce a streak, or you want to improve on the streak you have, don't get too caught up in the philosophy of everything, make sure your hypotheses feel like they're good, but my recommendation is just try things. And this is, again, you said it earlier, it's like this is as much human psychology as anything, and as soon as that becomes the case, you kind of just got to understand what users respond to. And the easiest way to do that is to stop spending time batting around ideas in a conference room and just try some stuff. So, huge recommendation to if you're going to invest in a streak, try and figure out what works through testing with users rather than trying to get it perfect on the first try.
turns.zh: 最后一点是，我们在Duolingo的连胜记录上做了大量测试，找出有效的做法。我们在Duolingo奉行先测试再行动的理念，愿意频繁测试新功能。我认为，如果你打算引入连胜记录功能，或是想改进现有功能，不要拘泥于理论框架，先确保假设合理。但我的建议是，大胆尝试。这再次印证了你之前的观点，用户心理因素至关重要。一旦意识到这一点，就要理解用户的反应方式。最简单的方法就是别再会议室里空谈想法，直接动手测试。所以，如果你要投入精力打造连胜记录功能，务必通过用户测试找出有效方案，而不是一开始就追求完美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say someone's listening and they're like, should we do streak, is this worth doing? What's your take on just the chances that a streak feature would be helpful to another consumer?
turns.zh: 假如有人听了这段讨论后想问：我们该不该引入连胜记录功能？这个功能对其他用户是否有价值？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: I am well known for saying in the company that I think every team, every app could benefit from a streak. Now, how you implement it is very different, and I think you got to, what is your user's use case? If they're going to come use, I don't know, tax software... Okay, you know what? Now that I say this, tax software would be a hard one, but maybe it's all about you need users to come back every day, during the tax season, or how many times... I don't know. Now, that I say this out loud-
turns.zh: 我在公司里出了名地喜欢说，每个团队、每款应用都能从连胜机制中获益。但具体如何实现却因应用而异。我认为首先要问自己：用户的使用场景是什么？如果他们要使用某款应用，比如税务软件……好吧，我知道税务软件是个难题，但关键在于你需要确保用户在报税季期间每天回访，或者达到特定次数……我也不确定。现在我把这些想法说出来——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Times you upload your [inaudible 01:19:37] forms.
turns.zh: 比如上传[1:19:37未听清]表格的次数。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, that is a hard use case. But the vast majority of companies I think have a good idea of like, all right, here is my ideal use case, I want users to come here three times a month, that would be ideal. Or four times a month. You can build a streak to work. Peloton has weekly streaks because the idea of doing a Peloton workout every single day was hard for this user during COVID. It was just like every now and then you get on the Peloton, that was great, but the idea of a weekly streak was something that I could keep up. And so, I think figure out what your usage pattern is, as a user, and then build your streak around it. But as long as you're not a really, again, the tax example is probably a good counterfactual, but as long as you have some degree of frequency in your use, I think almost anything can have a streak.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个难题。但我认为绝大多数公司都能清楚自己的理想用户画像。比如，理想情况下，用户每月来访三次或四次。围绕这个频率来设计连胜机制即可。不过除非是像税务软件这种用户粘性极低的场景，否则只要有一定的使用频率，几乎所有应用都能引入连胜机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, Duolingo, it's, again, a $14 billion company, this feature, possibly the most contributing factor, other than the core product, to that level of success in market cap, and it's hard to imagine another just feature of a product that has had this much impact on growth and revenue and building this sort of business. So, I love that we spent this much time on it, the motherload, the motherload of advice and insights. So, thank you again for putting-
turns.zh: 拿Duolingo来说，这家市值140亿美元的公司，其连胜机制可能是除核心产品外，对市值贡献最大的功能。很难想象还有哪款产品功能能对增长、营收和商业模式构建产生如此深远的影响。所以我很欣慰我们能花这么多时间探讨这个核心功能，真是宝藏般的建议与洞见。再次感谢你们的付出——

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Of course. Very fun.
turns.zh: 当然。非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，您向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: All right, I'll start with A Guide to Midwest Conversation. So, I'm based in Kansas City, I'm a proud Midwesterner, and us Midwesterners talk in a certain way. I think you hear about Minnesota nice, but we tend not to say what we mean, and it is a very funny primer into what Midwesterners actually mean when they say what they say. So, highly recommend reading that.
turns.zh: 好的，我先说《中西部对话指南》。这本书让我深有共鸣，作为堪萨斯城人，我为身为中西部人而自豪。我们这儿的人说话方式独特。大家都听说过“明尼苏达式友善”，但我们往往会含糊其辞。这本书用幽默的方式解析中西部人说话的深层含义，强烈推荐一读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that you give that to people, just like, here's what I might be telling you, which you may not read.
turns.zh: 我喜欢把它送给别人，比如说，告诉他们：看，我现在可能正在跟你们说这些，但你们未必会读。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: My wife is German, and I gave it to her so she could better understand.
turns.zh: 我妻子是德国人，所以我送给她让她能更好地理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see German being the opposite of that, okay.
turns.zh: 我发现德国人恰恰相反，哈哈。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Very different. Another book, this is a good one, Fate is the Hunter. This is a really cool book, it's a memoir of one of the early commercial airline pilots, and it is wild to hear the stories about what flying was back in the day. I'm a former management consultant, I flew every week for almost six years, and I never once had to worry about, am I going to make it to the other end of this flight alive? That was not the case back then, and so some of the stories about what it used to be like to be a pilot on some of these planes, before modern aviation technology, is fascinating, and makes you really appreciate what we have.
turns.zh: 截然不同。另一本书，这本很棒，叫《猎手命运》。这是一本超酷的回忆录，讲述了一位早期商业航空公司的飞行员的故事。听那些关于过去飞行生活的故事真是令人惊叹。我曾是一名管理顾问，几乎六年间每周都要飞行，但从未担忧过能否安全抵达目的地。那时的飞行环境与现在不可同日而语。因此，回顾那些在现代航空技术尚未普及的时代当飞行员的经历，真是令人着迷，也让我们更加感激如今所拥有的一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels good to read a book like that, being a software PM or engineer or whatever, how different that life is.
turns.zh: 读这样一本书感觉很棒，作为软件项目经理或工程师，我们的生活与之相差太大了。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Hardware is hard.
turns.zh: 硬件开发太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hardware. Oh man, it's not haptic design. Okay. Next, unless there's any other books you're going to share? No, okay, great. What's a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 硬件开发。天哪，这可不是什么触觉设计。好的，接下来你有没有其他想分享的书？没有的话，好的，很棒。你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: So, I have two kids, I watch a lot of Bluey, it's really good, I swear, it brings me no shortage of joy. But adult show or show not meant for four-year-olds that I have watched, I just finished the latest season of Emily in Paris, man, wonderful. I realize it's not the highest brow of television, but just beautiful people in beautiful cities, solving problems that are not earth-shattering, sometimes it is nice to just tune out. Also, I'm learning French on Duolingo, slight plug for the app, I can understand a lot of the French that is being spoken, and there is no better joy than having invested as much time as I have in French, and actually being able to use it. So, huge fan of Emily.
turns.zh: 我有两个孩子，经常看《蓝色小精灵》，那部动画真的很棒，我发誓它总能给我带来无尽的欢乐。但说到成人剧或不适合四岁孩子看的节目，我刚看完最新一季的《艾米丽在巴黎》，天哪，太棒了。我知道这部剧不算高雅，但就是美丽的城市里漂亮的人们解决着不算惊天动地的问题，有时放松一下也不错。另外，我在Duolingo上学习法语，顺便推荐一下这个应用，我能听懂不少法语了，能把投入这么多时间学到的法语知识实际运用出来，真是再开心不过了。所以，我超爱《艾米丽在巴黎》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so funny, what a fun Venn diagram of interests. My mother-in loves Emily in Paris, I saw someone tweeting about what Visa is she on? How is she still in Paris?
turns.zh: 太有趣了，真是兴趣爱好交集的趣味图。我的岳母超爱《艾米丽在巴黎》，我看到有人在推特上问她用的是什么签证？她怎么还在巴黎？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah. You best just not ask questions, there's a lot of questions for this show that are better left unasked.
turns.zh: 是啊。你最好别问问题，这部剧有很多疑问，还是不问为好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 01:23:40] Okay. Do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you really like? Other than Duolingo.
turns.zh: [01:23:40听不清]好的。你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？除了Duolingo以外。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Last week I went to Home Depot, and I bought a new ladder, and ladder innovations, you don't think of often, but you can make one of the legs go a little bit further than the other leg. And as somebody like myself who has a house that is built on a slight slope, every time I go up on my ladder, I take my life in my hands, but with this ladder, I'm always even. I cleaned my gutters twice last week just because of how awesome this ladder has... How much this ladder has changed my life. So, ladder innovation, I don't think it gets talked enough about and so I'm happy to give it the spotlight it deserves.
turns.zh: 上周我去家得宝买了把新梯子，梯子设计的创新之处你可能想不到，但你能让其中一条腿比另一条长一点。像我这样房子建在斜坡上的家伙，每次爬梯子都是冒险，但用这把梯子，我总能保持平衡。上周我清理了两次排水沟，就因为这把梯子太棒了……它真的改变了我的生活。所以，梯子设计的创新值得大书特书，我很高兴能让它得到应有的关注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate you doing that, and it's the first ladder recommendation we've had on the podcast. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you really find useful in work or in life they share with folks?
turns.zh: 感谢你分享，这也是我们播客上首次推荐梯子。最后两个问题。你有没有在工作或生活中特别实用的人生格言可以分享？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: This probably will not be much of a surprise based on how I've talked about our willingness to test things, but you miss 100% of the shots that you don't take. I'm a big fan of just trying things, even if your possibility of success is not 100, because you learn a lot along the way.
turns.zh: 基于我之前提到的我们乐于尝试新事物的态度，或许这并不令人意外。但如果你不尝试，就注定会错过所有机会。我非常赞成勇于尝试，即便成功概率不达100%，因为在探索的过程中你总能收获宝贵经验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, do you have any fun traditions at Duolingo, amongst either the PM team or the company in general that might be delightful to share?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题：在多邻国（Duolingo），无论是产品经理团队还是整个公司，是否有任何有趣的传统，值得分享一下？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: We have way too many traditions to count. I will share the weird tradition that we do at every retention standup, and this started during the pandemic, we obviously used to stand up in person, and then when we went remote, we did this thing where whoever's the last person to go would count down 3, 2, 1, and then we'd all try to clap at the same time, which was kind of fun and dorky, but we fell in love with it, and four years later we're still doing it. Recently we've added, we all say yee-haw in unison afterwards, I can't tell you why. But trying to synchronize a clap via Zoom, and then all shouting yee-haw... I did this in a phone booth the other day and after I came out someone told me, "You know that those aren't as soundproof as you think," but when you get a good opportunity to give a yee-haw, you can't pass up on it, so.
turns.zh: 我们这里的传统多到数不清。我想分享一个在每周留存会议上流行的奇特传统。这始于疫情期间——我们原本是面对面开会，但转为远程后，大家会轮流倒计时：最后一个发言的人会喊“3、2、1”，然后所有人齐声鼓掌。虽然有点幼稚但很有趣，我们至今仍在延续这个传统。最近我们又增加了一个环节：所有人统一喊“耶哈！”虽然不知道为什么，但通过Zoom同步鼓掌，再集体高呼“耶哈！”——这种体验太棒了。前几天我在电话亭试了一下，结果有人提醒我：“你以为电话亭隔音效果很好？” 但既然有机会喊“耶哈”，怎么能错过呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love these little things, they sound so minor, but they're such important elements of team culture and tradition, and so important for PMs to find ways to just have fun and do something ridiculous.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这些小传统。它们看似微不足道，却是团队文化和传统的重要元素。对于产品经理来说，找到让团队欢笑、做些疯狂事情的机会至关重要。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: I will say, it took a while to get people behind shouting yee-haw, but now that we have people doing it, you can't take it away [inaudible 01:26:08], we all love it.
turns.zh: 说实话，刚开始让大家接受喊“耶哈”挺难的，但现在大家都乐在其中，再也离不开了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I called our all hands for a while, y'all hands, feel free to steal that.
turns.zh: 天哪，我主持的全员会议也喊过“耶哈”，大家随意借鉴吧。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: You get it, you get it Lenny. Yeah.
turns.zh: 懂的，懂的，伦尼。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I get it. Jackson, this is incredible, I feel like people are going to listen to this with notebooks, and just like, okay, here's a bunch of ideas we should try with whatever we're working on, whether it's streaks or not. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more, learn more about Duolingo? I know you're hiring product managers, so share more there, and finally, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我明白了。杰克逊，这太棒了。我觉得听众听完后，肯定会拿着笔记本记下这些点子，然后想：“好吧，无论我们在做 streaks 功能还是其他项目，都可以借鉴这些思路。”非常感谢你的到来。最后两个问题：如果大家想了解更多信息，或者想加入多邻国团队，可以在哪里找到你？我知道你们正在招聘产品经理，欢迎分享更多信息。最后，听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yes, you can find me on LinkedIn, that is where most of my online social media is, so Jackson Shuttleworth, and then how people can be useful to me, yes, as you said, we are hiring. We're actually hiring for my team. Are you interested in thinking about streaks as much as we do? We might be the right home for you, so please, you can apply on our website. We're also hiring from a number of other product management roles, and they're all as thrilling as this work is. (01:27:05): And then, I'm always interested about how other companies have implemented streaks and what they've learned, and so what I'd say is if you're a company who's implemented a streak maybe in a different way than Duolingo has, or you found a whole ton of success and another vector, another element of the feature that we didn't talk about today, I would love to know more. I used to catalog basically every streak I found out there, and as it's become more of a popular feature, it's just been hard to keep up on. So, if you have interesting streak insights to send my way, I would love to hear them.
turns.zh: 是的，你可以在领英上找到我，那里是我大部分线上社交媒体的聚集地，所以我的账号是Jackson Shuttleworth。至于人们如何能为我提供帮助，正如你所说，我们正在招聘。我们实际上是在为我的团队招人。你是否和我们一样对连续日期挑战（streaks）充满热情？我们或许正是适合你的团队，所以请在我们的网站上申请。我们还招聘其他多个产品管理职位，这些职位都和这项工作一样令人兴奋。（01:27:05）：另外，我一直很想了解其他公司是如何实施连续日期挑战的，以及他们从中获得了哪些经验。所以我想说，如果你的公司以不同于多邻语的模式实施了连续日期挑战，或者你发现了巨大的成功案例，或者找到了我们今天没有讨论过的功能的其他维度或元素，我很乐意了解更多信息。我过去曾基本整理了所有我发现的连续日期挑战案例，但随着它越来越受欢迎，跟上更新已经变得很困难了。所以，如果你有有趣的连续日期挑战见解想分享给我，我很乐意倾听。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that, a collection of all the best ways of doing streaks. Jackson, just I want to say congrats to your team and you for having so much impact. This is like the dream of a lot of PMs and teams, is to see this much impact and continue to ship wins, and so congrats, nice work.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个想法，把所有优秀的连续日期挑战案例都收集起来。杰克逊，我只想祝贺你的团队和个人能产生如此大的影响。这是许多产品经理和团队的梦想——看到如此大的影响力并持续交付成果，真是太棒了。恭喜你，干得好。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Thank you very much.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks for [inaudible 01:27:59]. And with that, Jackson, thanks so much for being here.
turns.zh: 感谢你[01:27:59的发言]。好的，杰克逊，非常感谢你今天的到来。

turns.speaker: Jackson Shuttleworth
turns.en: Yeah, thank you Lenny, this was a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 是的，谢谢你，莱尼，今天的交流非常愉快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same. Bye everyone. turns.zh: 我也是。再见大家。（01:28:07）：非常感谢你的收听。如果你觉得这期节目有价值，可以在Apple Podcasts、Spotify或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅我们的节目。另外，请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，这真的能帮助其他听众找到我们的节目。你可以在Lenny'sPodcasts.com上找到所有过往节目或了解更多信息。下期节目见。
